To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the non-biochemical antioxidant BHT: 1) was a repellent in choice tests with two sub-terranean termite and one drywood termite species; 2) was a feeding repellent in no-choice tests with two subter-ranean termite species; and 3), in outdoor ground-contact field trials, BHT-treated wood stakes were less degraded by termites than untreated control stakes.

a man-made antioxidant, BHT, was an effective termite feeding repellent and a termite mortality inducer in no-choice laboratory experiments, and in field trials BHT-treated stakes had less termite damage than the control stakes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that the antioxidant properties of extractives are responsible for the termite avoidance and mortality observed with extractive-containing wood.

the hypothesis that termites avoid wood with high antioxidant properties and that this is a second property, in addition to termite toxicity, of wood extractives that affects termite resistance and mortality.
the hypothesis that wood extractives, and specifically the non-biocidally active antioxidant properties of some extractives, affect termite behavior and cause termite mortality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the antioxidant property of wood extractive compounds is a major factor in the termite resistance of wood and that this resistance is due to the antioxidant interfering with termite and microbial digestion of lignin.
the presence of antioxidants, whether natural or synthetic, in wood or wood products, is sufficient to repel and kill subterranean termites.
the antioxidant properties of natural and manmade extractives and/or antioxidants, respectively, interfere with the termites and their symbiotic microbes ability to digest lignocelluloses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the antioxidant properties of natural wood extractives are an important factor affecting termite resistance and that artificial and benign antioxidants will be a useful tool to further investigate this hypothesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the antioxidant properties of extractives are a second non-biochemical property of wood extractive that can affect termite mortality and behavior.

the use of a non-biocidal and nontoxic compound, BHT, as an antioxidant, can be used to definitively test the hypothesis that wood extractives with antioxidant properties are a second factor that affects termite mortality.
the use of a non-biocidal, artificial antioxidant, in combination with other non-biocides, could be used to enhance the resistance of wood to termites.
